title: AI Candidate Screening With Reasoning Behind Every Score
h1: AI candidate screening where every score shows its reasoning
desc: AI candidate screening works when every score shows its reasoning and the source text from the résumé, so the recruiter can check it and make the decision.
lead: AI candidate screening is useful when every score comes with the reasoning behind it and the exact lines from the résumé it was based on. The recruiter reads the evidence, agrees or disagrees, and makes the decision. A score with no reasoning is a guess the team cannot check.
short: A score is only useful if the recruiter can see why it was given.
Each score should point to the source text in the résumé, word for word.
The software ranks and drafts; the recruiter decides and approves.
Outreach drafted from a candidate's own work is read and approved before it is sent.

sections.h2: What is AI candidate screening with reasoning?
body: It is a way of reading a batch of résumés against a role where the software explains itself. For each candidate it gives a score, a short written reason for that score, and the passage from the résumé that supports it. Nothing is hidden behind a number.
The point is not to replace the recruiter's judgment. The point is to take the first pass of reading, comparing and sorting off the team's desk, while keeping every step open to inspection.
This approach suits any firm that reads applications in volume, from an independent recruiter to an established search firm. It is a reading aid, not an automatic filter.
In practice, the recruiter sees the following side by side for every candidate:
The score against each requirement of the role.
A plain sentence saying why the score was given.
The source text: the exact lines from the résumé the reasoning rests on.

sections.h2: Why does a bare score not help a recruiter?
body: A ranked list with numbers looks tidy, but it raises more questions than it answers. Why is this candidate ahead of that one? Did the software miss a line on page two? Was a job title read too literally?

Without the reasoning, the recruiter has two choices: trust the number blindly or reread every résumé to check it. The first is risky with a client's search. The second removes the reason for using the software at all.

When the reasoning and the source text sit beside the score, checking takes a glance. If the reasoning is wrong, the recruiter can see it and overrule it. If it is right, the recruiter moves on with confidence.
The same applies when a client asks about a shortlist. A consultant who can point to a line in a résumé gives a stronger answer than one who can only point to a number.

sections.h2: How does Vero show the reasoning and the source text?
body: Vero is recruiting software made by Loose Ends as one of its own products. It reads a batch of résumés against a role and ranks the candidates. Every score it gives comes with the reasoning and the source text behind it.
The work it takes on is the slow, repetitive part of a search:
Reading each résumé against the role, rather than skimming for keywords.
Ranking the candidates so the strongest appear first.
Showing, for every score, why it was given and which lines it came from.
Drafting outreach to each candidate from that candidate's own work, not from a generic template.
The decision stays with the recruiter. Vero prepares the shortlist and the drafts; a person reads them, changes what needs changing, and approves each message before it is sent.
Because the outreach draws on what the candidate has actually done, it reads as a message written for that person. The recruiter can still rewrite it completely; the draft is only a starting point.

sections.h2: How is a candidate assessed against a search's own criteria?
body: Every search is different. A board role, a technical lead and a regional manager do not share one checklist, and a firm's clients often have requirements that never appear in a job advert.

For this reason Loose Ends has also built a candidate assessment system for client work that scores candidates against the criteria of a specific search, not a general template. The firm sets the criteria. The system reads each candidate against them and writes its reasoning beside each score.

This matters for two reasons. The recruiter can defend a shortlist to the client, because each placement on it has a written reason. And when the criteria change halfway through a search, the candidates can be read again against the new ones, with the reasoning updated to match.

sections.h2: What does reasoning beside a score look like?
body: Take a sample role that asks for experience running a regional sales team. A sample candidate's score on that requirement comes with a short reason, such as having led a team across several offices, and beneath it the sentence from the résumé that says so. If the résumé mentions selling but not leading, the reasoning says that too, and the score reflects it.

This is sample data, written to show the format. The same format makes mistakes easy to spot: if the quoted line does not support the claim, the recruiter sees the mismatch at once and corrects the score.

sections.h2: Who makes the decision, the software or the recruiter?
body: The recruiter. This is a design rule in every system the studio builds: the software drafts and prepares, and a person approves before anything is sent to a client or a candidate.
In a screening workflow, that rule looks like this:
The software reads, scores and ranks, and shows its reasoning.
The recruiter reviews the ranking and overrules any score that is wrong.
The software drafts outreach for the candidates the recruiter chooses.
The recruiter reads each draft, edits it if needed, and approves it before it goes out.
This keeps the firm's name and judgment on every message. It also means a mistake in the software is caught by a person before it reaches anyone outside the firm.

sections.h2: What does a firm need before it starts screening this way?
body: Less than most teams expect. The résumés are usually already in a recruiting system or a shared folder. The role description exists. What is often missing is a written list of what the firm actually looks for, beyond the advert.

Writing that list down is useful on its own: it makes the criteria clear to everyone on the team, and it gives the screening something precise to read against. From there, the screening can sit inside the tools the firm already uses rather than adding another login. To see where screening and the rest of a search lose time in a particular firm, Loose Ends offers a free one-page review, with no call required.

faq.q: Does AI candidate screening make the hiring decision?
faq.a: No. The software reads, ranks and explains its scores. The recruiter reviews the reasoning, overrules what is wrong and makes the decision.

faq.q: What is source text in candidate screening?
faq.a: It is the exact passage from the résumé that a score is based on. Showing it lets the recruiter check the reasoning in seconds instead of rereading the whole document.

faq.q: Are outreach messages sent automatically?
faq.a: No. Drafts are written from each candidate's own work, and a person reads and approves every message before it is sent.

faq.q: Can the screening use a firm's own criteria?
faq.a: Yes. The candidate assessment system scores candidates against the criteria of a specific search, set by the firm, with the reasoning written beside each score.

title: Sync Job Listings From an ATS to the Firm's Website
h1: Sync job listings from the recruiting system to the firm's website
desc: Open roles can be entered once in the firm's recruiting system and appear on its website automatically, with no retyping. CVs can be reformatted in one step.
lead: A firm can enter each open role once, in its recruiting system, and have it appear on its own website without anyone retyping it. When the role changes or closes in the recruiting system, the website follows. The same connection can put candidate CVs into the firm's format in one step.
short: Roles are entered once, in the recruiting system the team already uses.
The website reads from that system, so listings never drift out of date.
Candidate CVs are put into the firm's own format in one step.
An executive search firm in Washington D.C. works this way today.

sections.h2: What does syncing job listings from an ATS to a website mean?
body: An ATS, or applicant tracking system, is the recruiting software where a firm keeps its roles, candidates and notes. Loxo is one example. Syncing means the firm's website reads the open roles directly from that system instead of someone copying them across by hand.
The recruiting system becomes the single place where a role is written. The website shows what is there. Nobody has to remember to update two places.

The same idea works for any business that keeps listings in one system and shows them in another, whether roles, properties or courses. The system of record stays in charge, and the website follows it.

sections.h2: Why is retyping job listings a problem?
body: Copying a role from one system into a website editor looks like a small chore. In practice it is a chore that repeats for every new role, every edit and every closed search, and it is usually done by whoever has a spare moment.
The usual results are familiar to most recruiting teams:
A role that closed weeks ago is still on the website, and candidates keep applying.
A salary range or location is updated in the recruiting system but not online.
A new role goes live late because nobody had time to copy it.
Small differences in wording creep in between the two versions.
None of these is dramatic on its own. Together, they make the website less reliable than the system behind it, and they take time from people who should be talking to clients and candidates.

Retyping also hides the real state of a search. When the website and the recruiting system disagree, nobody is sure which is right, and a consultant has to check before answering a candidate's question.

sections.h2: How does the connection between the recruiting system and the website work?
body: The website asks the recruiting system for the current list of open roles and shows them in the site's own design. Most recruiting systems, Loxo included, offer a way for other software to read their data. Where no ready connector exists, Loose Ends builds a custom integration to the system's API, the interface it provides for other software.
A typical setup covers these points:
Which roles are public and which stay internal, decided by a field in the recruiting system.
Which details appear online: title, location, summary, and anything else the firm chooses.
What happens when a role closes: it leaves the website without anyone touching the site.
How a candidate applies, and where that application lands in the recruiting system.
The team keeps working in the recruiting system exactly as before. The only change is that the website is no longer a second job.

sections.h2: How can candidate CVs be reformatted in one step?
body: Search firms usually present candidates to clients in their own format: a consistent layout, the firm's branding, and sections in a fixed order. Candidates send CVs in every format imaginable. Turning one into the other is often done by hand, line by line.

The same connection can take a CV from the recruiting system and produce a version in the firm's format in one step. The content comes from the candidate's own CV; the layout comes from the firm. A consultant reads the result and approves it before it is sent to a client.

Because the layout is fixed, every CV the client receives looks the same, which makes candidates easier to compare side by side. Consultants spend their time on the summary and the judgment, not on fonts and margins.

sections.h2: Case: an executive search firm in Washington D.C.
body: An executive search firm in Washington D.C. now enters its open roles in its recruiting system, Loxo, and they appear on its website without anyone retyping them. The website was built by Loose Ends.

Candidate CVs are put into the firm's format in one step. The same database also answers the team's questions through their AI assistant: the recruiting database and the firm's internal chat are connected to the assistant, so a consultant can ask about a role or a candidate without searching by hand.
The website is live. Candidate scoring, which reads candidates against a search's criteria and shows its reasoning, is in development.

sections.h2: Can an AI assistant read the same recruiting data?
body: Yes, if it is connected to it. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is an open standard introduced by Anthropic in November 2024 for connecting AI assistants such as Claude to tools and data. Through a connector, the assistant can read the recruiting database the website already reads from.
This turns the database into something the team can question in plain language, for example:
Which open roles have had no new candidates this month?
Which candidates in the database have worked in a given sector?
What was last agreed with a client about a search?
The assistant answers from the firm's own records. Anything it drafts for a client or a candidate is read and approved by a person before it is sent.
Because the assistant and the website read the same records, they never disagree with each other. Keeping the recruiting system up to date becomes the one job that keeps everything else right.

sections.h2: What should a firm check before connecting its systems?
body: A few things are worth confirming early: whether the recruiting system allows other software to read its data, which fields the team actually keeps up to date, and who decides when a role is public. It also helps to know which searches the firm keeps confidential, since some roles are never advertised. With those settled, the connection is a contained piece of work, and the firm keeps ownership of the code, domain and accounts. To see where retyping and copying cost a particular firm the most time, Loose Ends offers a free one-page review, with no call required.

faq.q: Can Loxo job listings appear on a firm's own website?
faq.a: Yes. The website can read open roles from Loxo and show them in the site's own design, so roles are entered once and never retyped.

faq.q: What happens when a role closes?
faq.a: When the role is closed or marked internal in the recruiting system, it leaves the website without anyone editing the site.

faq.q: Does reformatting a CV change what the candidate wrote?
faq.a: No. The content comes from the candidate's CV and the layout comes from the firm. A consultant checks and approves the result before it goes to a client.

faq.q: What if the recruiting system has no ready connector?
faq.a: Loose Ends builds a custom integration to the system's API, so the website and the AI assistant can still read from it.

title: Interview Notes to Client Report, Every Rating Sourced
h1: Turning interview notes into a client report in the firm's format
desc: Raw interview notes can become a finished client report in the firm's format, with every rating pointing to its source and gaps flagged, never filled in.
lead: Raw interview notes can be turned into a finished client report in the firm's own format, where every rating points back to the line in the notes it came from. Where the notes say nothing, the report says so, instead of filling the gap. A consultant reads and approves the report before it goes to the client.
short: The report follows the firm's own format, section by section.
Every rating points to the passage in the notes that supports it.
Missing information is flagged for the consultant, never invented.
A person approves the report before it is sent to the client.

sections.h2: What does turning interview notes into a client report involve?
body: After an interview, a consultant usually has a page of rough notes, a transcript or a recording summary. The client expects something else: a clean report in the firm's format, with ratings against the role's criteria and a clear recommendation.

Getting from one to the other means reading the notes again, sorting each remark under the right heading, rating each criterion, and then retyping it all into the firm's template. The system Loose Ends has built does that sorting and drafting, and leaves the judgment to the consultant.
The approach is not limited to recruiting. Any firm that turns conversations into written assessments, such as advisers writing up client meetings, has the same chore and can use the same rules.

sections.h2: Why does writing client reports by hand take so long?
body: The thinking happens in the interview. Most of the time afterwards goes on chores that do not need a consultant's experience:
Reading back through notes to find what the candidate said about a given topic.
Copying quotes and observations into the right section of the template.
Retyping headings, names, dates and role details that already exist elsewhere.
Checking the format matches the last report sent to the same client.

These chores also make reports uneven. Two consultants writing about the same candidate will order things differently, and a busy week shows in the result. A system that drafts in a fixed format gives every report the same structure before the consultant adds their view.
Reports also tend to be written last, because they are the task most easily pushed to the end of the day. A draft that is already in the right shape makes that last task smaller.

sections.h2: How does every rating point to its source?
body: Each rating in the draft report carries a reference to the passage in the interview notes it was based on. If the report says a candidate is strong on leading a team through change, the consultant can see the exact remark from the interview that supports it.

This does two things. It lets the consultant check every rating quickly, without rereading the whole set of notes. And it lets the firm stand behind the report if a client asks why a candidate was rated the way they were.
Sourcing also protects the candidate. A rating rests on what they said, not on an impression that cannot be traced, and an unfair rating is easier to catch.
A rating with no source behind it does not appear as a rating. It appears as a question for the consultant.

sections.h2: What does a sourced rating look like?
body: Here is a sample entry, written to show the format:
Criterion: leading a team through a reorganisation.
Rating: strong, on the firm's own scale.
Reasoning: the candidate described running the reorganisation of a department and how they kept people informed.
Source: the line in the interview notes where this was said, linked so the consultant can open it.

This is sample data. A real report follows whatever rating scale and wording the firm already uses. If the consultant disagrees with a rating, they change it, and the source stays attached so anyone reading the file later can see what the rating was based on.

sections.h2: What happens when the notes leave a gap?
body: Interviews rarely cover every criterion. Time runs out, the conversation goes elsewhere, or a topic is left for a second meeting. A careless system would fill that gap with something plausible. This one does not.
When the notes say nothing about a criterion, the draft report marks it clearly:
The criterion is listed with no rating.
A note explains that the interview did not cover it.
The consultant decides whether to follow up with the candidate, rate it from other knowledge, or leave it open in the report.
Gaps are flagged, never filled. This is the rule that makes the rest of the report trustworthy: whatever is in it came from the interview.
Flagging gaps also shows where the interview itself could be tighter. If the same criterion is flagged across several candidates, the firm can add it to its interview guide.

sections.h2: Where do the notes come from, and where does the report go?
body: The system works with the material the firm already has. Notes can be typed by the consultant, taken from a transcript, or drawn from an interview recording tool such as BrightHire. The firm's report template and rating scale are set once.

The finished draft can be filed against the candidate in the firm's recruiting system, such as Loxo, so the report and the candidate record stay together. Nothing has to be copied from one place to another by hand.

The format itself belongs to the firm. Headings, rating scale, the order of sections and the wording of the recommendation are taken from the reports the firm already sends, so clients see no change in style.

sections.h2: Who approves the report before the client sees it?
body: A consultant, every time. The system drafts and prepares; a person reads the report, adjusts ratings where their judgment differs, fills or confirms the flagged gaps, and approves it before it is sent to the client.

The consultant's name goes on the report, so the consultant has the last word on everything in it. The system's job is to make that last read quick and well supported, not to replace it. Over time, reports also become more consistent across consultants, because every draft starts from the same structure and the same rules. To see where reporting and other repeated writing cost a particular firm the most time, Loose Ends offers a free one-page review, with no call required.

faq.q: Can AI write a candidate report from interview notes?
faq.a: It can draft one in the firm's format, with each rating linked to the passage in the notes it came from. A consultant reviews and approves the report before it is sent.

faq.q: What if the interview did not cover a criterion?
faq.a: The report flags the gap and leaves the rating empty. The consultant decides how to handle it; the system never fills it in.

faq.q: Does the report use the firm's own template?
faq.a: Yes. The firm's format and rating scale are set once, and every report is drafted to match them.

faq.q: Can the notes come from an interview recording tool?
faq.a: Yes. Notes can be typed, taken from a transcript, or drawn from a tool such as BrightHire, as long as the firm can export or connect to them.

keywords: AI candidate report from interview notes

title: Shopify Etsy Inventory Sync Without Selling Twice
h1: Keeping Shopify, Etsy and spreadsheets in step
desc: Shopify and Etsy inventory stays in sync when stock lives in one place and every sale updates it, so an item is never sold twice and nothing is retyped.
lead: To keep Shopify and Etsy inventory in sync, stock should be counted in one place, and every sale on either shop should update that count straight away. Both shops then read from the same number, so an item cannot be sold twice. Orders, listings and spreadsheets follow the same rule, so nothing has to be retyped.
short: Pick one place where the true stock count lives.
Every sale on Shopify or Etsy updates that count, and both shops follow it.
Listings are written once and published to both shops.
Spreadsheets read from the same data instead of being typed up by hand.

sections.h2: Why do Shopify and Etsy stock counts drift apart?
body: Shopify and Etsy each keep their own stock count. Neither knows what the other has sold. When a business sells the same item in both places, the two counts only agree if someone updates them by hand after every sale.

That works on a quiet week. It stops working when orders come in at night, during a busy season, or while the person who does the updating is away. The result is an item shown as available in one shop after its last unit has already sold in the other.
The same drift happens with prices, descriptions and photos. Each shop is edited separately, so small differences build up between what the business thinks it sells and what customers actually see.

sections.h2: What goes wrong when stock is managed by hand?
body: The problems are rarely large, but they repeat:
The last unit sells twice, and one customer has to be contacted, apologized to and refunded.
Orders are copied from each shop into a spreadsheet, and a line is missed or entered twice.
A price or description is changed in one shop and not the other.
Items made to order are listed as in stock because the production list lives somewhere else.
Time goes on checking and correcting rather than making and selling.
Each of these is a chore that exists only because the systems do not talk to each other. Connecting them removes the chore rather than speeding it up.
There is also a cost in trust. A customer who receives a refund instead of the item they ordered may not order again.

sections.h2: How does a Shopify and Etsy inventory sync work?
body: Both Shopify and Etsy let other software read and update their data through an API, the interface each platform provides for that purpose. A sync uses those interfaces to keep one shared record of stock and to push changes to both shops.
In a typical setup:
One place holds the true stock count for each item. It can be Shopify itself, a spreadsheet or a small database.
When an order arrives on either shop, the count is reduced in that one place.
Both shops are updated from the new count, so the item shows the same availability everywhere.
When stock is added after a delivery or a production run, it is entered once and both shops follow.
The rule underneath is simple: one count, many shop windows. Whatever the business already uses can stay, as long as it agrees on which record is the true one.

If something does not match, for example an item sold in one shop that is missing from the other, the sync flags it for a person to check rather than guessing. A person stays in charge of anything unusual.

sections.h2: Can listings and orders stay in step too?
body: Yes. The same connection that carries stock can carry listings. A product is written once, with its photos, description and price, and published to both shops. A later change to the price or description is made once and appears in both.

Orders can flow the other way: from each shop into one list, with the customer, the item and the shop it came from. Nothing is copied by hand, and the team works from a single order list instead of checking two dashboards. Any message to a customer, such as a delay notice, is drafted from the order and approved by a person before it is sent.

Order data can also feed a weekly report: what sold, through which shop, and what is running low. The report is prepared automatically and read by the team, so decisions about restocking rest on current figures.

sections.h2: Where do spreadsheets fit in?
body: Many businesses keep a spreadsheet for stock, sales and production because it is flexible and everyone can read it. There is no need to give that up. The spreadsheet can read from the shops automatically, so it stays current without anyone typing orders into it.

For businesses that want to start with a spreadsheet before connecting anything, Loose Ends offers a free stock, sales and production tracker at https://houssem-gabsi.vercel.app/tools/stock-sales-production-tracker/. For businesses that make their own products, the production side matters as much as the shops. A connected spreadsheet can show what has sold, what is left, and what needs to be made next, in one view.

sections.h2: Which businesses need a Shopify and Etsy sync?
body: Any business that sells the same items in more than one place: a maker with an Etsy shop and its own Shopify store, a retailer with a counter and an online shop, or a studio selling prints alongside commissions. The size of the business matters less than the number of places its stock is shown. Once stock appears in two places, it can be wrong in one of them.

sections.h2: What should a business decide before connecting its shops?
body: A few decisions make the work clear from the start:
Which record holds the true stock count.
Whether every product is sold in both shops, or only some.
How made-to-order items and limited runs are shown.
Who on the team approves anything sent to customers, such as delay or refund messages.

It is also worth listing every place stock is held, including market stalls and wholesale orders, since the count must account for all of them. Once these are settled, the connection is built around the tools the business already has. The code, accounts and data belong to the business. To see where stock, orders and listings cost a particular business the most time, Loose Ends offers a free one-page review, with no call required.

faq.q: Can Shopify and Etsy share one stock count?
faq.a: Yes. A sync keeps one true stock count and updates both shops whenever an order arrives or stock is added, so the same item shows the same availability in both.

faq.q: Does the business have to stop using its spreadsheet?
faq.a: No. The spreadsheet can read from both shops automatically, so it stays current without anyone typing orders into it.

faq.q: Can product listings be written once for both shops?
faq.a: Yes. A listing can be written once and published to Shopify and Etsy, and later changes to price or description appear in both.

faq.q: Are customer messages sent automatically?
faq.a: No. Messages such as delay or refund notices are drafted from the order, and a person approves them before they are sent.

keywords: sync stock between Shopify and Etsy

title: Booking App Instead of Instagram Messages: Why Switch
h1: Why bookings should move from Instagram messages to one booking screen
desc: A business that takes bookings through Instagram or WhatsApp messages should move them to one booking screen showing schedule, places, payment and language.
lead: A business that takes bookings through Instagram or WhatsApp messages should move them to a single booking screen, because messages are a poor place to keep a schedule. One screen can show the schedule, the places left, the payment and the choice of language, so customers book themselves. The team stops answering, confirming and chasing each booking by hand.
short: Messages scatter bookings across chats; one screen keeps them in one place.
Customers see the schedule and the places left, and book without waiting for a reply.
Payment is taken at the moment of booking, not chased afterwards.
The screen can work in more than one language, such as French and English.

sections.h2: Why do bookings through Instagram or WhatsApp messages cause problems?
body: Messaging apps are built for conversation, not for keeping a schedule. Every booking becomes a short exchange: is there a place, what time, how to pay, can a friend come too. Each exchange has to be answered by a person, often outside opening hours.

The schedule itself ends up in someone's head, a notebook or a spreadsheet updated after the fact. When two people ask for the last place at the same time, there is no single record to settle it. Message-based booking also depends on whoever holds the phone. When that person is teaching, travelling or unwell, bookings wait.

Messages also get lost. A booking request sinks under newer chats, a reply is read but not answered, and a customer arrives for a session that was never confirmed. For the customer the experience is uncertain too: they wait for a reply before they can plan.

sections.h2: What chores does a booking screen take away?
body: Most of the work in message-based booking is not the booking itself. It is everything around it:
Answering the same questions about times, prices and places.
Confirming each booking by hand, one message at a time.
Chasing payments that were promised in a message and never arrived.
Copying bookings from chats into a calendar or a list.
Telling people a class is full after they have already planned to come.
A booking screen handles these in one place. The customer sees what is available, picks it, pays, and receives a confirmation. The team sees the result instead of producing it.

It also frees the business's messages for the conversations that need a person: a question about an injury, a group booking or a special request. Those conversations get more attention once the routine ones are gone.

sections.h2: What should one booking screen show?
body: A good booking screen answers every question a customer would otherwise send as a message. For most businesses that take bookings, that means:
The schedule: what is on, and when.
The places: how many are left for each session.
The payment: taken at the moment of booking, so a place is only held once it is paid for.
The language: the same screen in each language the customers speak.
The confirmation: a clear message after booking, with the details the customer needs.
It should work well on a phone, because that is where the customer was when they would have sent the message. Ideally it fits on a single screen, so booking takes less effort than writing a message.

Payment at booking also makes cancellations simpler. When a place has been paid for, the rules are clear to both sides from the start. Clear prices and session details on the same screen also answer many questions before they are asked.

sections.h2: Case: a yoga studio's bookings on a single phone screen
body: A yoga studio was taking bookings through Instagram messages. Loose Ends built a booking application that puts the schedule, the places and the payment on a single phone screen, in French and English.
Bookings moved out of Instagram messages into one place. Students choose a class, see whether there is room, and pay in the same screen, in the language they prefer. The application is live.

sections.h2: Does moving bookings off Instagram mean leaving Instagram?
body: No. Instagram and WhatsApp remain good places to be found and to talk with customers. The change is only that the booking itself happens somewhere built for it.

In practice, the profile, the posts and the replies all point to the booking screen. When someone asks about a class in a message, the answer is a link rather than a back-and-forth. Any reminders or follow-up messages the system drafts can be set so that a person approves them before they are sent.

Instagram also stays useful for news about the schedule: a new class, a change of time, a special session. Each post can link straight to the screen where the place is booked. This keeps the personal side of messaging while removing the admin around it.

sections.h2: What about reminders and cancellations?
body: Once bookings live in one place, reminders can come from the same record. A note before the session, a message when a place frees up, or a notice when a class moves can all be prepared by the system. A person approves the wording of each message before it is sent.
The same record makes cancellations easier to handle. A cancelled place returns to the schedule at once, so the next person can book it instead of asking in a message whether anything has opened up.

sections.h2: What does a business need to decide before building a booking app?
body: A booking application is built to order, around how the business already works. A few questions shape it:
What is being booked: classes, rooms, appointments or something else.
How places are counted, and what happens when a session is full.
How payment is taken, and the rules for cancellations.
Which languages the screen needs.
Who on the team looks after the schedule once it is live.

A booking screen is also a record: over time it shows which sessions fill first and which have room, so the schedule can be planned from real bookings. The answers decide the screen, not the other way round. The code, domain and accounts belong to the business, and handover includes training and a named owner for each routine. faq.q: Why not keep taking bookings through Instagram messages?
faq.a: Messages scatter bookings across chats and need a person to answer, confirm and chase each one. A booking screen keeps the schedule in one place and lets customers book themselves.

faq.q: Can a booking app take payment?
faq.a: Yes. Payment can be taken at the moment of booking, so a place is only held once it is paid for.

faq.q: Can the booking screen work in more than one language?
faq.a: Yes. The yoga studio's booking screen works in French and English, and other languages can be added the same way.

faq.q: Does the business still use Instagram?
faq.a: Yes. Instagram stays the place to be found and to talk with customers. Its profile and replies point to the booking screen.
